meta.title: Prediction intervals that remain valid for unseen alloy families: family-calibrated conformal prediction for machine-learned alloy properties
meta.description: Manuscript for Journal of Materials Research and Technology

blocks.text: Prediction intervals that remain valid for unseen alloy families: family-calibrated conformal prediction for machine-learned alloy properties

runs.t: Machine-learning models are increasingly used to screen alloys from chemical systems that have never been measured, yet their uncertainty estimates are validated on randomly held-out alloys. We show that this practice fails under alloy-family extrapolation. Across 6 public datasets (multi-principal-element alloy hardness and yield strength, steel yield strength, and three inorganic-compound properties), nominal 90% conformal intervals calibrated on random splits covered only 85–87% of alloys from unseen chemical systems and 72–86% from unseen composition clusters. We propose family-calibrated conformal prediction (FCP): CV+ intervals whose calibration folds hold out whole alloy families, with scores normalized by a leakage-free scale built from family-bagged ensemble disagreement and compositional novelty. A family-weighted variant targets family-level coverage, and the finite-sample condition for its validity is stated explicitly. In 180 evaluation runs (6 datasets × 3 split protocols × 10 seeds) against eight interval methods, FCP restored mean coverage to 0.922 and 0.902. It reduced the coverage shortfall relative to seven baselines and the interval score relative to six (Holm-corrected Wilcoxon tests). Ablations identify family-grouped calibration as the decisive component. Random-forest tree-spread intervals were competitive under shift, but only because they systematically over-cover in-distribution. Remaining failures concentrate in alloy families with extreme property values. All results are reproducible from public data with the released code.
Alloy design; High-entropy alloys; Machine learning; Uncertainty quantification; Conformal prediction; Out-of-distribution generalization; Materials informatics

items.t: Random-split 90% conformal intervals cover only 72–87% of new-family alloys
Family-grouped CV+ calibration restores nominal coverage on new alloy families
Leakage-free scale from ensemble spread and novelty adapts the interval width
Benchmark: 6 datasets, 3 shift protocols, 17 interval methods, 10 seeds
Remaining misses concentrate in alloy families with extreme property values

runs.t: Machine-learning (ML) models that map alloy composition and processing to properties are now routinely used to screen candidate alloys before synthesis, including high-entropy and other multi-principal-element alloys (MPEAs) [1–3]. The candidates of greatest interest are usually

close relatives of the alloys in the training data: a design campaign typically moves into chemical systems, or regions of composition space, that have never been measured. For such decisions a point prediction is insufficient. An alloy designer needs an interval that contains the true property with a stated probability, so that design margins, screening thresholds and experimental budgets can be set rationally [4,5].

Conformal prediction converts any point predictor into prediction intervals with a finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantee [6–8]. The guarantee rests on one assumption: the calibration data and the new case must be exchangeable. In the usual workflow, calibration alloys are drawn at random from the same database as the training alloys. When the new alloy belongs to a family that is absent from that database, exchangeability fails at precisely the point where the prediction is most needed [9]. Materials studies have shown that randomly split cross-validation overstates accuracy for new chemistries [10–13]. Recent work on polymers has shown that split-conformal coverage falls well below nominal when whole chemical classes are held out [14,15]. For composition-based alloy property models, however, the size of this coverage loss has not been quantified, and no calibration procedure has been proposed and tested that remains valid when the test alloy comes from an unseen alloy family.
This paper addresses that gap. We treat the
(the chemical system of an alloy, or a cluster of similar compositions) as the unit of exchangeability, following the hierarchical view of Dunn et al. [16]. On this basis we construct

. FCP calibrates a cross-validation-plus (CV+) interval [17] on residuals of whole held-out families. The scores are normalized by a scale that grows with ensemble disagreement and compositional novelty, and the scale model is fitted only on family-out-of-bag residuals, so calibration labels are never reused. A family-weighted variant (FCP-W) targets equal coverage across families instead of across alloys. We evaluate both against eight established interval methods on six public datasets, under three split protocols of increasing extrapolation difficulty.

items.t: A calibration procedure, FCP / FCP-W, whose calibration step reproduces the deployment shift of alloy design (prediction for an unseen alloy family). It states its estimand explicitly (alloy-level vs family-level coverage) and the finite-sample condition under which the family-level interval is finite (Section 4).

A benchmark of interval coverage under alloy-family extrapolation: 6 tasks, 3 split protocols, 10 outer-split seeds and 17 interval methods. It shows how far random-split calibration and model-based uncertainty fall below nominal coverage (Section 7).

Ablation, robustness, sensitivity and efficiency experiments that isolate which component matters and what it costs, together with an error analysis of the alloy families on which intervals still fail (Sections 8–11).
A fully reproducible code base in which every number, table and figure is regenerated from public data by a single command.

blocks.text: 2.1. Uncertainty quantification for materials property models

runs.t: Uncertainty estimates for materials ML are most often model-based. They include the spread of random-forest trees or bootstrap ensembles [5,18], Gaussian-process (GP) posterior variances [19], and the dispersion of neural-network ensembles, Monte-Carlo dropout or evidential heads [13,20,21]. Comparative studies report that such estimates are frequently miscalibrated, and they recommend recalibrating them on held-out data [22,23]. Recalibration uses randomly held-out data, however, so it inherits the exchangeability problem examined here. Benchmarks of out-of-distribution (OOD) prediction for crystal structures [12,13] and for out-of-range property values [24] document accuracy losses and moderate uncertainty–error correlations. They do not evaluate the coverage of prediction intervals.

Conformal prediction has recently been applied to materials data. Boruah [25] used split, normalized, Mondrian and quantile-based conformal methods for the fatigue strength of steels. That study showed that marginal validity can hide under-coverage in the highest-strength quartile, but all of its evaluations used random splits of a single dataset. For polymers, Akdoğan [15] and Han et al. [14] evaluated split conformal prediction under scaffold, cluster and class holdouts. Han et al. reported that coverage fell from 0.899 under random splits to 0.683 under class holdout, and that a similarity-based applicability gate gave little protection. Neither study proposed a calibration procedure that restores coverage under the holdout.

Statistical work offers several routes beyond exchangeability. Weighted conformal prediction reweights calibration scores by an estimated density ratio under covariate shift [26,27]. Bounds on the coverage lost under non-exchangeability are available [9]. Methods also exist that target conditional or group-wise coverage [28,29]. Dunn et al. [16] studied two-layer hierarchical data, in which groups are exchangeable but observations within a group are not exchangeable with those of other groups, and constructed prediction sets for observations from a

group. Locally adaptive (normalized) conformal scores [7,30,31] and cross-conformal / CV+ constructions [17,32] make intervals adaptive and data-efficient. To our knowledge these tools have not been combined and tested for the alloy-family extrapolation problem.
Three observations motivate this work. (i) Alloy design is an extrapolation problem at the level of

: new chemical systems, or new regions of composition space. (ii) The standard calibration step of conformal prediction draws calibration alloys at random, so it measures interpolation error. Its guarantee therefore does not transfer to new families, and the size of the resulting shortfall for alloy property models is unknown. (iii) Weighted conformal prediction corrects covariate shift only when the test distribution has support inside the calibration distribution. A genuinely new chemical system violates that condition, so it is unclear whether density-ratio weighting helps.
We therefore ask five research questions.
: do random-calibrated conformal methods and model-based intervals keep their nominal coverage on unseen chemical systems and composition clusters?
: does family-level calibration close the coverage shortfall, and at what cost in interval width?
: which component of FCP is responsible: grouping, normalization or weighting?
: is the procedure robust to label noise, smaller training sets, the miscoverage level and its own hyper-parameters?

: does it generalize across datasets and shift types, including a mis-specified family definition? Each question is answered by a pre-specified experiment (Section 6), and the design was fixed before the main results were inspected.

runs.t: Six regression tasks from public sources were used (Table 1). Two come from the MPEA database of Borg et al. [34]: Vickers hardness, and yield strength with test temperature, test type (tension/compression) and processing route as additional inputs. One is the yield strength of 312 steels from Matbench [35]. Three are inorganic-compound tasks, used to test generalization beyond alloys: the bulk modulus training set of Mansouri Tehrani et al. [36] (rows flagged as suspect removed), experimental formation enthalpies compiled by Kingsbury et al. [37], and superconducting critical temperatures from the SuperCon-derived dataset of Hamidieh [38]. Identical inputs (same formula and, for MPEA tasks, same processing and test conditions) were merged by the median target before any split. The superconductor set was reduced to 4007 compounds by sampling whole chemical systems with a fixed seed, to fit the computational budget. Fig. 2 shows the target distributions and the strongly skewed sizes of the chemical-system families: most systems contain one or a few alloys, a few contain dozens.

runs.t: The primary level was α = 0.1, with α = 0.05 and 0.2 secondary. The unit of statistical analysis is a cell: one task under one shift protocol, averaged over the ten seeds. Seeds re-partition the same data, so they describe split-to-split variability, not independent replicates. Pre-specified hypotheses were tested with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests over the 12 shift cells (6 tasks × 2 shift protocols), and Holm correction was applied across the eight baselines. H1 tested one-sided under-coverage of random-calibrated methods against 0.90. H2 tested FCP against each baseline on the coverage shortfall max(0, 0.9 − coverage). H3 tested the same comparisons on the interval score. Effect sizes are matched-pairs rank-biserial correlations, and 95% confidence intervals for the median paired difference were obtained by bootstrap (10,000 resamples). The two shift protocols of a task share data, so the 12 cells are not fully independent. Each test is therefore also reported separately per protocol (6 cells).
Pre-specified settings: LightGBM with 200 trees, learning rate 0.07, 15 leaves, row and column subsampling 0.8 and 0.5;

= 5; 16 principal components. None of these was tuned on test folds, and their influence is examined in Section 9.3. All computations ran on CPUs (4 cores, no GPU) with Python, scikit-learn [44] and LightGBM. A single command (run_all.py) regenerates every number, table and figure from the public data.

Each research question was mapped to one pre-specified experiment, and each claim in Sections 7–11 refers to one of them. Exp. 1 (main evaluation, RQ1–RQ2): all methods × 6 tasks × 3 protocols × 10 seeds × α ∈ {0.05, 0.1, 0.2}. Exp. 2 (baselines): the eight comparison methods of Section 5.4 within Exp. 1. Exp. 3 (ablation, RQ3): ten CV+ variants that differ only in fold grouping, scale model and weights. Exp. 4 (robustness, RQ4): Gaussian label noise of 0.10 and 0.25 SD(y), and training on 50% of the training families (system protocol, 5 seeds). Exp. 5 (generalization, RQ5): a mis-specified family definition in which FCP calibrates on chemical systems while the test shift is composition clusters, together with a base-learner swap to random-forest members and a random (unbalanced) assignment of clusters to outer folds. Exp. 6 (computational cost): wall time and peak memory per outer fold. Exp. 7 (sensitivity): one-factor-at-a-time variation of
. Exp. 8 (error analysis): per-family coverage against novelty, property extremity and family size.

Holding out whole families degraded the shared point predictor in every task (Table 2). Mean R² over tasks fell from 0.847 (random) to 0.769 (unseen chemical system) and 0.516 (unseen composition cluster). The largest losses occurred for steel yield strength (R² 0.74 → 0.12) and superconductor Tc (0.89 → 0.22). The two protocols therefore represent moderate and severe extrapolation, respectively.

blocks.text: 7.2. RQ1: random-split calibration does not transfer to unseen families

runs.t: In the random protocol, every conformal method attained its nominal 90% coverage (Fig. 3, left; Table 3). Mean coverage was 0.901 for SCP, 0.917 for CV+, 0.899 for CQR and 0.905 for WCP. The same methods under-covered as soon as whole families were held out: 0.851, 0.869, 0.851 and 0.874 for unseen chemical systems, and 0.719, 0.743, 0.747 and 0.863 for unseen composition clusters. The worst cell fell to 0.637 (SCP). Over the 12 shift cells, the one-sided Wilcoxon test rejected nominal coverage for all four methods (H1: p = 0.0002, 0.0012, 0.0002 and 0.0171). Their median cell coverages were 0.803, 0.824, 0.826 and 0.871, respectively.

Density-ratio weighting (WCP) reduced the shortfall, but only by producing unbounded intervals: 9.5% (system) and 41.5% (cluster) of its intervals were infinite. This happens because the classifier assigns the test alloys of a new family density ratios that dominate all calibration weights. Weighting cannot repair a support mismatch; it can only make it visible. Among the model-based intervals, the GP covered 0.887 and 0.821, and the base ensemble's own spread (Ens-z) covered only 0.481 and 0.454. Family-subsampled bagging thus does not by itself produce calibrated uncertainty. Random-forest tree spread (RF-z) is discussed in Section 7.4.

Horizontal bars are means over datasets; the dashed line is the nominal level. Colour encodes the method group and marker shape the individual method.

runs.t: FCP attained mean coverage 0.922 on unseen chemical systems and 0.902 on unseen composition clusters. Its worst cells were 0.915 and 0.851. In the random protocol it was conservative (0.941), as expected: calibrating on whole held-out families measures extrapolation error even when the test alloys are not extrapolations. FCP-W, which targets family-level coverage, attained family coverage 0.925 under the system protocol, against 0.912 for FCP and 0.837 for SCP. Under the cluster protocol only eight training clusters remain per outer fold, below the bound of Eq. (10), so 64% of its intervals were infinite by construction.

Over the 12 shift cells, FCP's coverage shortfall max(0, 0.9 − coverage) was significantly smaller than that of seven of the eight baselines after Holm correction (H2, Table 4; p_Holm ≤ 0.020; rank-biserial r = −1 for six of them). The median paired reductions ranged from 1.0 to 42.5 percentage points. Compared with the simplest family-calibrated alternative, GSCP, which holds out 25% of the families for split calibration, the median reduction was small (1.0 points) but consistent (p_Holm = 0.012). Its effect was concentrated in the cluster protocol, where GSCP covered only 0.816 because it calibrates on a few held-out clusters, whereas CV+ uses every training family once. The only baseline whose shortfall did not differ from FCP's was RF-z (p_Holm = 0.50).

Coverage alone can be bought with width. The interval score, which penalizes both width and misses, was significantly better (lower) for FCP than for SCP, CV+, CQR, GP, Ens-z and GSCP (H3; p_Holm ≤ 0.042). WCP could not be scored because it returned infinite intervals in 11 of the 12 cells. FCP's intervals were wider than those of the random-calibrated methods (mean width 1.47 vs 1.20 SD(y) for CV+ under the system protocol; 2.64 vs 1.31 under the cluster protocol; Fig. 4). The extra width is the price of covering extrapolation error that the narrower intervals miss: their miss penalties outweigh the width saving.

blocks.text: 7.4. A strong heuristic competitor: random-forest tree spread

runs.t: RF-z deserves separate discussion. Its coverage was as high as FCP's under both shifts (0.950 and 0.914), and its interval score was lower on average, although the difference was not significant (median paired difference +0.146 SD in favour of RF-z, p_Holm = 0.077). RF-z is not calibrated, however. It over-covered in the random protocol (0.955 at a nominal 0.90; 0.911 at a nominal 0.80, against 0.873 for FCP), and individual datasets reached 0.98. Its apparent robustness therefore comes from intervals that are systematically too wide in-distribution. That inflation happens to offset the extrapolation error under shift, but nothing guarantees it. It depends on forest hyper-parameters such as max_features and leaf size, and it cannot be dialled to a requested level. Section 9.4 asks the constructive question: does family-level calibration applied to a random-forest point predictor combine the forest's efficiency with calibrated coverage?

runs.t: Interval validity matters for decisions. A common use of intervals in alloy design is to accept a candidate only if even its pessimistic (lower-bound) prediction exceeds a target. We emulated this under unseen-chemical-system holdout: an alloy was 'selected' when its lower bound exceeded the upper quartile τ of the property (Table 5). Pooled over five tasks and ten seeds, 4.6% of the alloys selected with SCP and 3.4% of those selected with CV+ were false discoveries, against 1.2% with FCP. For MPEA yield strength the false-discovery proportion fell from 18% (SCP) to 7% (FCP). The gain is not free: FCP recovered 28% of the true high performers against 38% for SCP. RF-z was more conservative still (false discoveries 0.3%, recall 20%), and CQR's wide quantile intervals almost never cleared the threshold. With family-level calibration, the stated confidence of a lower-bound screen holds on new chemical systems; with random-split calibration, it is overstated by a factor of three to four.

caption.t: Table 5.

Screening for high performers under unseen-chemical-system holdout (α = 0.1). An alloy is selected if the lower bound of its interval exceeds the upper quartile τ of the task's property. Per task: mean number selected per seed / false-discovery proportion (selected alloys with measured property < τ). Pooled over 5 tasks × 10 seeds: false-discovery proportion (FDP) and recall of all alloys with property ≥ τ.

runs.t: Table 6 and Fig. 6 decompose FCP into its three design choices: family-grouped folds, the scale model (none, spread only, novelty only, both) and family weights.

Switching CV+ from random to family-grouped folds, with nothing else changed, raised mean coverage from 0.869 to 0.920 (system) and from 0.743 to 0.893 (cluster). Over the 12 shift cells the median gain was 9.1 percentage points (Wilcoxon p = 0.0005). Normalization

grouping (NCV+, analogous to the normalized conformal method used for steels with random splits [25]) narrowed the intervals but did not fix coverage (0.884 and 0.857). FCP covered more than NCV+ in the paired comparison (median +4.0 points, p = 0.016).

The two difficulty signals play different roles. The ensemble spread improved efficiency: the interval score of GCV+[spread] was 1.937 vs 2.082 (system) and 3.324 vs 3.457 (cluster) for the unnormalized grouped CV+. Compositional novelty instead improved coverage for the most novel alloys. In the highest novelty tertile under cluster holdout, coverage was 0.932 for FCP against 0.878 for GCV+ (12-cell median difference +3.7 points, p = 0.0015; Fig. 7). Novelty also widened the intervals, so that under the cluster protocol FCP's interval score (3.539) was worse than spread-only normalization (3.324). Over the 12 cells, the FCP vs GCV+ interval-score difference was not significant (p = 0.47). Hence the pre-specified 'both' scale buys more uniform coverage across novelty levels at a modest efficiency cost. A user who values average efficiency over conditional coverage should prefer the spread-only scale.

Family weights (the -W variants) raised family-level coverage (FCP-W vs FCP: median +4.4 points, p = 0.0049) at the cost of wider intervals. They also became unbounded when fewer than nine training families were available, as Eq. (10) predicts.
Revision history of the scale model.

The first version of the scale model (v1) extrapolated the log-linear fit beyond the range of the difficulty signals seen during fitting. It produced a few extremely wide intervals for test alloys with rare processing categories or compositions. Clamping the signals to their fitting range (v2, used throughout) left coverage unchanged (FCP, alloy tasks, cluster protocol: 0.919 vs 0.918) and left the median width unchanged (2.82 vs 2.81 SD). It reduced the mean width from 6.64 to 2.93 SD and the interval score from 7.36 to 3.70 (Supplementary Table S1). The change was made after the interim analysis, and it is documented together with the original results.

runs.t: To see where intervals still fail, coverage was computed for every test family with at least five alloys in the system protocol (all seeds pooled; Fig. 8, Table 7). The dominant failure mode was

, not compositional novelty. For FCP, within-family coverage decreased with the family's mean distance from the median target (|y − median|/IQR) in 5 of 6 tasks (Spearman ρ from -0.44 to 0.05). The families in the most extreme sextile were covered 0.82 of the time by FCP, against 0.64 by SCP. FCP therefore reduced this failure substantially but did not remove it. The association with novelty was weaker and of inconsistent sign, which suggests that, once calibration is family-level, the remaining misses are dominated by regression toward the mean of the training labels for families with unusually high or low properties. Fig. 9 illustrates this for MPEA hardness: the uncovered alloys concentrate above about 800 HV.

Table 7 lists the families with the lowest FCP coverage. Several are metallurgically distinctive within their datasets. Examples in the MPEA yield-strength data are the Cr–Fe–Ni–Ti and Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Mo–Ni systems and the refractory Nb–Ta–Ti and Al–Mo–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr systems. The ensemble predicted their strength levels poorly: the mean absolute error of the worst family exceeded 1159 MPa. An Fe–As–O–Sm (iron-pnictide) family appears among the superconductors, and maraging-type Co–Fe–Mo–Ni–Ti steels among the steels. These are cases in which a new strengthening or pairing mechanism, absent from the training families, governs the property. No calibration of residuals can anticipate such a mechanism. FCP's intervals are honest about the
extrapolation error over families, not about every individual family.

runs.t: What the results mean for alloy design.

A materials-informatics workflow that reports 'conformal' 90% intervals calibrated on random held-out alloys delivered, on average, 85–87% coverage on new chemical systems and 72–75% on new regions of composition space. In the worst datasets coverage was close to two-thirds. The nominal level is therefore not a property of the method alone. It is a property of the method

of how the calibration data relate to the deployment data. The remedy studied here is simple to state: calibrate on whole held-out families, so that the calibration residuals measure the kind of error the model will make in use. With that change, coverage on unseen families returned to the nominal level on average. The price is intervals about 23% (system) and 102% (cluster) wider than the under-covering random-calibrated ones. Measured by the interval score, which accounts for both width and misses, that price was worth paying in every comparison except against random-forest tree spread.

The family is the unit of novelty against which coverage is certified. Chemical systems are natural for HEA/MPEA design campaigns that open new element combinations. Composition clusters are natural when moving to distant regions of an existing system. Section 9 shows what happens when the definition used for calibration is coarser or finer than the actual shift. Practitioners should calibrate at the level of novelty they intend to explore. With few families, they should prefer unweighted FCP, whose interval stays finite, over FCP-W, whose interval correctly becomes unbounded.

The coverage collapse reported for polymer chemistry holdouts [14,15] is reproduced here for alloys and inorganic compounds, across six datasets and two kinds of family shift. Normalized scores, which restore label-conditional coverage under random splits in steels [25], do not restore coverage under family shift unless the calibration folds are grouped (NCV+ vs FCP, Section 8). Density-ratio weighting [26] is unsuitable when the test family lies outside the support of the calibration data, as is typical of alloy discovery. The family-level construction follows the hierarchical view of Dunn et al. [16], adapted to cross-fitting, normalized scores and a leakage-free scale model.

For screening alloys from unexplored families, (i) define families from composition before modelling; (ii) calibrate with family-grouped folds (FCP), or at minimum with a family-held-out calibration split (GSCP) when data are plentiful; (iii) report the coverage obtained under a family-holdout evaluation, not under random cross-validation; and (iv) treat alloys with predicted properties far outside the training range with extra caution, because that is where the remaining misses concentrate (Section 11).

items.t: No new finite-sample theorem is proved for the full normalized, family-weighted CV+ construction. Validity on new families is assessed empirically on six datasets, and it rests on the families being approximately exchangeable units. A design campaign that deliberately moves
away
from all known families (adaptive or feedback shift [27]) violates this assumption.
Coverage is marginal over alloys (FCP) or over families (FCP-W), not conditional on an individual alloy. Families with extreme properties remained under-covered (Section 11).

Under the cluster protocol only ten families exist per dataset. Family-level (FCP-W) statements at α = 0.1 are then impossible (Eq. 10), and the outer partition of the balanced protocol is identical across seeds (Section 9.5).

All datasets are public compilations. MPEA entries from different publications differ in processing and testing details that are only partly encoded, and inter-laboratory bias cannot be separated from model error.

Features are composition-based (plus processing and test conditions for MPEA). Microstructure, defect and thermomechanical-history descriptors, which govern many mechanical properties, were not available.
Superconductor data were subsampled to about 4,000 compounds by whole chemical systems to fit the computational budget (4 CPU cores). Results for the full set may differ quantitatively.

Hyper-parameters were fixed defaults and were not tuned per dataset. Tuning would raise point accuracy for every method alike and is unlikely to change the calibration comparison, but this was not tested.

runs.t: Prediction intervals for machine-learned alloy properties were examined in the setting that matters for discovery: prediction for alloys from families absent from the training data. The main conclusions are:

items.t: Conformal intervals calibrated on randomly held-out alloys lose their guarantee under alloy-family extrapolation. Nominal 90% intervals covered 0.85–0.87 of alloys from unseen chemical systems and 0.72–0.86 from unseen composition clusters.

Family-calibrated conformal prediction (FCP), i.e. CV+ with family-grouped folds and a leakage-free, novelty-aware scale model, restored mean coverage to 0.922 and 0.902. It reduced the coverage shortfall relative to seven of eight baselines and improved the interval score relative to six.

Grouping the calibration folds by family is the decisive ingredient. The ensemble-spread scale improves efficiency, and the compositional-novelty scale equalizes coverage across novelty levels at a small efficiency cost.
Random-forest tree-spread intervals were an unexpectedly strong but uncalibrated competitor. Their robustness comes from systematic over-coverage in-distribution.

Remaining failures concentrate in families with extreme property values, where new strengthening or pairing mechanisms are likely. Interval estimates for such candidates should be treated with additional caution.
